The AI Act handles contrary-to-duty obligations (CTDs) involving temporality by stating that certain properties used to be fulfilled but no longer are. An example provided is where a notifying authority must investigate if a notified body no longer meets the requirements laid down in Article 31. This situation is reformulated to show that the obligation to fulfill the requirements is only necessary at one point in time before being notified, and if the notified body no longer fulfills these requirements, it does not equate to a violation of the previous obligation.

To represent such cases, the suggested logic is Dyadic Deontic Logic (DDL), which differentiates between ideal and actual obligations and introduces a conditional obligation operator, allowing for the expression of CTDs that arise when ideal obligations have been violated. Additionally, a logic that can express temporality, such as Temporal Logic, is also relevant for capturing the notion of time in these obligations.
